newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - UK budget, Japan data and lira in focus.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - UK budget, Japan data and lira in focus.

text.p: Japanese data and Britain's keenly awaited budget will be the market highlights in the week ahead, analysts said on Friday. Italy will also be in focus after it requested a lira re-entry to the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
In a week when U.S. data releases are scant, markets can still expect action-packed trading sessions, they said.
Along with a raft of economic data during the week, all eyes will be on Japan's "Tankan" survey of business sentiment for the fourth quarter, due on Tuesday.
"This will be a crucial clue as to what the (Japanese) economy's doing and as to where interest rates might go," said Sonia Gibbs, bond strategist at Nomura International in London.

Gibbs said Nomura forecast the Tankan index to be minus seven against the general market expectation of around minus two. She said the index would show enough strength in the economy to cause anxiety about the pace of Japan's recovery.
"I think it will probably be enough in the current environment for JGBs to be nervous," she said.

Other data from Japan include retail sales on Wednesday, industrial production on Thursday, and consumer prices, unemployment and housing starts on Friday. Analysts said they did not expect to see a significant rise in Japanese inflation.
The Japanese bond market must also absorb an injection of supply with 10-year bonds up for auction on Monday.
"I don't think many investors will want to go long into the Tankan," said Adam Chester, international bonds strategist at Yamaichi International in London.
Attention will also be on Italy after it called for a meeting of the European Monetary Committee at the weekend.

Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio said on Friday the government had been working hard to be ready for monetary union at the planned 1999 start date. Speculation of a lira re-entry to the ERM has been in the markets for weeks.
"If the lire re-entered this weekend and the Bank of Italy dropped rates, we'd have a hell of a lot of good news," said Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets.

He said markets would also be waiting for further news from the Italian government on their proposed "Euro tax" -- a one-off tax designed to bring the country within the Maastricht criteria for participation in the single European currency.

In Britain all markets are awaiting the 1997/98 budget on Tuesday. Analysts said they expected Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to be prudent after the recent 25 basis point rise in British interest rates.
They said politics were not at the top of Clarke's agenda and that he was more concerned with controlling the government deficit and avoiding another interest rate rise.
"That would be good news for the short end of the gilts market," said McDevitt who is based in London.

"But it could actually be negative for sterling," he said. "The market could realise that even though rates are going up, it'll probably be a lot slower. We might only get one more 25 basis point rise before the election."
Britain is due to hold a general election by May 1997.
Analysts said they thought a cut in taxes would not necessarily be damaging for the gilts market.
"If he doesn't deliver a neutral budget the gilt markets will take it reasonably well. The market's priced in a fair bit of good news already," said Chester.

Nomura's Gibbs said she would watch the spread between BTPs and gilts to gauge sentiment towards EMU. The spread of BTPs over Bunds recently fell below the gilt-Bund spread for the first time ever, illustrating the yield premium in the British market for not being committed to EMU, analysts said.
From the U.S., the revision of third quarter GDP data is due on Wednesday. Gibbs said she expected a downward revision to 1.7 percent growth from 2.2 percent before.
U.S. consumer confidence figures are due on Tuesday and both personal income and personal spending indices on Friday.
Analysts said they would be looking for signs of increased spending in the run-up to Christmas but on the whole they expected a quiet week from the U.S.
More regional inflation data are expected from Germany during the week. Analysts said they thought it would be subdued.
